newsitem.title: UK: Australia top pick in dollar bloc.
newsitem.headline: Australia top pick in dollar bloc.

text.p: Australian bonds have the most to gain against Treasuries within the dollar bloc despite a rosy fundamental outlook for the Canadian market, analysts said on Thursday.
"In Canada, much of the convergence is done and there is clearly a risk the next move in rates is up," Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase in London, said.
"In Australia, there is definitely a prospect the next move is down," he said.
Canadian bonds received a boost this week by the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision to leave interest rates alone.

The Fed's inaction took the pressure off the Bank of Canada to raise rates anytime soon. On Wednesday, yields of 10-year Canadian bonds shot to 28 basis points below 10-year Treasury yields, a new low.
Indeed, the fundamental background for Canadian bonds looks rock solid, according to Sonja Gibbs, senior bond strategist at Nomura International in London.
"There's no tension on the political front, no inflation, a wonderful fiscal deficit position," Gibbs said. "Canada is repeating this U.S. pattern of strong growth and low inflation."

Even the Canadian election on June 2 was expected to be a benign affair for the bond market. Opinion polls give Prime Minister Jean Chretien's Liberal Party a comfortable lead, although they are feeling the heat from the Conservatives in Quebec and the east.
Meanwhile, Treasuries were likely to be held hostage to data releases, Gibbs said, adding Wednesday's U.S. trade data did not bode well.
The U.S. trade gap shrank 19.3 percent to $18.5 billion in March. Gibbs said data like that gives a GDP estimate of close to 6.5 percent, well off the government's initial estimate of 5.6 percent.
"When that hits the tape we might have a little bit of a setback," she said.
Nevertheless, Gibbs said she did not expect the Canada/U.S. gap to make much headway from current levels and she too favoured Australian bonds.
Marshall at Chase expected the 10-year Australian/U.S. gap to slim to around 80 basis points from 99 now on a three month view.
He added interest rate cuts may be some time in coming but they should eventually feed through.
"The wage data overnight was a little disappointing but the evidence in the labour market is that wage pressures are not going to get passed through into final prices," he said.
Data on Thursday out of Australia showed private sector wages growth accelerated 1.3 percent in the three months to end-February from 0.8 percent in the previous three months.
The Australian Treasury threw cold water on the private sector data, saying wages growth was closer to the 1.0 percent figure shown for all sectors wages growth.

Michael Derks, cross market fixed income strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, favoured both Australia and New Zealand, saying they were the last of the high yielders among the major bond markets.
"Real yields in Australia are still very high," Derks said. "If you factor in two percent underlying inflation you get real yield of 5.7 percent," he said, referring to 10-year yields.
